Camp Director David Hartry and staff planning a training event 


A Letter from the President 


Dear Friends: 

The summer of 1961 and the 
summer of 1970 have been most ex¬ 
citing for me as President of the Ca¬ 
nadian Camping Association. I have 
visited a great many camps and par¬ 
ticipated in camp programs with 
thousands of campers in Central 
and Eastern Canada. What a joy it 
has been to be with children of all 
walks of our Canadian life in their 
own camp setting! Prominent Camp 
Directors in Canada like John Lat¬ 
imer, Robert Lazanik, Sophia Dc- 
metelin, Zave Ettinger, Tony Fry, 
Ivan Robinson, Tom Creighton and 
Peter Harris were my hosts for my 
visits. 

The biggest camp I visited was 
B’nai Britli Camp in Ste. Agathe 
du Mont with over 800 people in 
camp at one time. Zave Ettinger is 
the big man who can handle a big 
job. Just around a few turns Bob 
Lazanik was involved with hun¬ 
dreds of people in Pine Valley’s 
week-long grey cup games! The 


event was more exciting than the 
real thing. John Latimer's staff was 
winding up a training session at 
Kilcoo and eagerly waiting for the 
little angels to arrive! The campers 
at Pine Crest YMCA Camp (To¬ 
ronto) were extremely busy when 
I arrived and Tony Fry seemed to 
have everything under control. Vis¬ 
iting these and many other camps 
too numerous to mention has been 
a rewarding experience for me. All 
that we believe in and all that we 
stand for was exemplified in these 
camps. 

In the next few months that lie 
ahead much is to be accomplished 
in our rapidly growing association. 
Winds of change are blowing 
throughout the field of camping in 
North America and we in Canada 
are feeling the effects. As an asso¬ 
ciation we will be called upon more 
and more to give leadership in our 
means of education. We will be 
called upon to assist in all aspects 
of education, recreation and outdoor 


environmental living. To get a grip 
on these changes, the development 
of our National office, and the rec¬ 
ognition of our role to play in the 
future are the primary and urgent 
concerns facing us at this time. 
Careful thought and action will be 
applied as we go into the future. We 
are a few people working for the 
welfare and benefit of thousands in 
Canada and we need the eager sup¬ 
port of all of our members. 

This is the first opportunity that 
I have had to say how much we ap¬ 
preciate the work of the Editor and 
Editorial Committee of our “Cana¬ 
dian Camping”. All of us are in¬ 
deed proud to have such a great 
means of communicating with one 
another. 

Hoping that your summer was 
successful and happy, I remain, 
Yours sincerely, 


David Hartry, President

de demarches nombreuses aupres du

nouvellement de 1’octroi de $30,- 
000.00 pour le secretariat provin¬ 
cial.

president de la section anglaise de 
l’A.C.Q. en mai dernier.

l’A.C.Q.C.A. s’est poursuivi durant 
tout Pete ’70. Environ 75 camps 
dans la section anglaise et la sec¬ 
tion frangaise ont ete visites par 
trois equipes d’inspecteurs.

d’hebergement tant des jeunes que 
des adultes tels que l’A.C.Q., les 
auberges de Jeunesse, les Bases de 
Plein Air et autres devraient s’ef- 
fectuer dans un avenir rapproche 
dans le but d’offrir a la population 
des normes de securite et d’hygiene 
ameliorees tout en laissant a chaque 
organisme son autonomie.

cances familiales a prix modique a

sariat une politique globale des 
problemes des vacances familiales.

ONTARIO by Stan Wild 

We are on the move . . . come 
November 1st we shall be relocated 
in bigger, brighter, more central of¬ 
fice space at 102 Eglinton Avenue 
East, Suite 203, Toronto 315. As 
always the welcome mat will be out 
for camping people from every prov¬ 
ince, so if you are in Toronto, come 
say hello. 

Ontario is hoping that C.C.A. 
will now follow through on the de¬ 
cision made at the last annual meet¬ 
ing, and accept their (Ontario's) 
invitation to share space. 

The summer saw the start of the 
new STANDARDS co-operative vis¬ 
its between C.C.A. members and the 
American Camping Association. As 
a result of arrangements made earl¬ 
ier this year between the Standards 
Committees of the two Associations, 
joint visits were made to two On¬ 
tario camps, visitors from both As¬ 
sociations met at the camps on a 
pre-arranged day, made their visit 
together and thus saved the camps 
concerned from having two visits 
in one year. (A.C.A. before accred¬ 
iting camps located outside of the 
U.S.A., now requires that such 
camps who wish to be a member of 
A.C.A. must FIRST become a 
member of the National Camping 
Association (where there is one of 
the country in which the camp site 
is located.) The new arrangement 
works well and should prove bene¬ 
ficial to all concerned. 

This summer saw the introduc¬ 
tion of MANDATORY STAND¬ 
ARDS and to make them easily un¬ 
derstood they were prepared in a 
new format. The format works so 
well that all of the O.C.A. standards 
will be re-written into it for the 
summer of 1971. This year all ac¬ 
credited camps will be REQUIRED 
to sign an undertaking to abide by 
the mandatory standards in their fu¬ 
ture operations. This undertaking 
to be signed before their member¬ 
ship renewal and Directory listing 
is approved. 

(Editors note : Stan Wild has now 
been moved up to the position of 
Executive Director of O.C.A., a title 
more in keeping with the many 
functions that he performs.)

Jack MacKenzie 


Jack MacKenzie first saw the light 
of day in Neepawa, Manitoba, but 
failed to reveal how many years ago. 
Education: University of Manitoba, 
B.Sc.; University of Toronto, B PHE 
(Physical and Health Ed.); Uni¬ 
versity of Toronto, BA; Michigan 
State, MA (Physical Education). 
For the past 13 years Jack has been 
Supervisor of Physical Education for 
the Regina Board of Education. Two 
years prior to that he held a similar 
job in Brandon, Manitoba. 

Jack s camping and love of the out 
of doors became intensified during 
summer work in the Yukon, Northern 
British Columbia and Northern On¬ 
tario. This provided opportunities for 
experiences in living and travelling 
and working in the out of doors, and 
as Jack says “was very influential in 
shaping an outdoor orientation to my 
outdoor thinking’’. 

Add to this, summers in camping in

Standards in Camping 

A paper presented to The Society of Camp Directors 
by David Palter, B.Sc., P.Eng., Camp Consultant, 

Wednesday, November 26th, 1969. 


In researching the activities of 
the O.C.A. Standards and Legisla¬ 
tive Committee back to the early 
1950's, I have discovered that then, 
as now, our aspirations and goals 
were to provide excellent camping 
for children, and to do the best 
job we could as Camp Directors. 

In the early days of Camping 
and up to quite recently the only 
sources of information available to 
us were through membership in a 
camping association; Ontario, Que¬ 
bec, American, etc., the meeting 
and convention functions of each 
association provides this informa¬ 
tion. 

Thus, camp directors are in a 
sense self-educating — firstly, pos¬ 
sibly as counsellors in camps other 
than their own; secondly, meeting 
with other camp directors and ex¬ 
changing information. This latter 
experience — the exchange of in¬ 
formation between directors came 
about very slowly prior to the Stan¬ 
dards Committee Visiting Program. 
This has been functioning for a 
little more than 10 years and there 
are a few directors who still do not 
volunteer for this excellent oppor¬ 
tunity to see how others in the field 
of camping operate and thereby in¬ 
crease their own knowledge. 

One may wonder what this has 
to do with Standards and Legisla¬ 
tion. In my opinion, when a camp 
director wants to improve the opera¬ 
tion of his camp he seeks guide 
lines or accepted principles of 
camping that have been tested by 
time and are required either by 
law (Health Department Regula¬ 
tions) or are mandatory for mem¬ 
bership in recognized camping as¬ 
sociations. Thus the Standards 
Program of Camp Accreditation by 
means of the Study of Desirable 
Camping Practices becomes an im¬ 
portant educational factor. 

To my regret, I have heard that 
some Camp Directors refer to a 
Standards Committee visit as an 
“Inspection.” This is unfortunate 
because in all the efforts of the 
Standards Committee to achieve 
Camp Accreditation, it has been 
stressed that the prime purpose of 
the visit was the exchange of ideas 


between directors. This was the 
reason that visitors were chosen 
from among camp directors who 
had a minimum of 5 years' exper¬ 
ience at the administrative level. 
These were the people who could 
properly join in exchanging exper¬ 
iences and ideas and would benefit 
themselves by the visit to neigh¬ 
bouring camps. I am sure you can 
recall die day when it was unheard 
of to go to see your competitor dur¬ 
ing the summer, or the winter for 
that matter. Directors met at arms 
length — fully extended — at 
association meetings. Now, and I 
can definitely attribute this to the 
visiting program, many new friend¬ 
ships have been created and a pro¬ 
fessional atmosphere has been 
achieved — witness this gathering 
tonight. 

As early as 1952, the Board of 
O.C.A. adopted accreditation of 
children's camps in principle. The 
problem was to work out the details 
that would be acceptable to the 
then active members of O.C.A. As 
we all know there seemed to be 
some slight disagreement on how to 
do this. 

The first attempt was by means 
of “Minimum Standards”, with 
which all camps would have to 
comply. Well — there is no mini¬ 
mum when it comes to the physical 
property, because some of the best 
camping can be practised with an 
axe and ingenuity in building a 
basic shelter. It was found that 
Minimums would not work and a 
Self-evaluation Questionnaire in 
1954 brought in 44 responses. 
O.C.A. was not going to cancel 80 
memberships because they would 
not reply to a Self-evaluation Ques¬ 
tionnaire. The Standards Chairman 
at that time, reported to the board 
of O.C.A. that he was very discour¬ 
aged. I quote the following from 
the archives of the Ontario Camp¬ 
ing Association: “A meeting of the 
Legislative Committee took place at 
the Park Plaza Hotel at noon on 
Thursday, March 7th, 1957. Those 
present: Mr. Lloyd Perry, Dr. J. 
Harry Ebbs, Mr. Irwin Haladner, 
Mr. W. E. Yard, Mrs. Ralph Ray- 
mer, Mr. W. B. Danson, Mrs. 
G. W. Flynn. 


RECOMMENDATION FROM 
THE LEGISLATIVE 
COMMITTEE 

“We recommend that the On¬ 
tario Camping Association endorse 
and encourage the formation of an 
association of professional camp 
directors. The object of this asso¬ 
ciation will be to provide a gov¬ 
ernment - recognized organization 
through which the public will be 
protected against the operation of 
children's camps by undesirable and 
untrained directors.” This recom¬ 
mendation was presented to the 
Executive Committee of Ontario 
Camping Association in 1957 and 
was approved in principle. The first 
official mention of Professional 
Status and an Organization for 
Professional Camp Directors dates 
back to 12 i /2 years ago. 

As a result of the foregoing rec¬ 
ommendation, on April 29th, 
1957, I was asked to assume the 
chairmanship of the Standards 
Committee and charged with the 
responsibility of initiating a pro¬ 
gram of accreditation. I do not wish 
to regale you with my trials and 
tribulations. It is sufficient to re¬ 
call that visiting came about on a 
friendly, voluntary basis, and those 
who joined the team of visitors 
usually learned to enjoy this one or 
two day change of activity during 
the camping season — it was my 
day off from my own camp when I 
could spend some time with a fel¬ 
low camp director and see his camp 
in action. In return, every third or 
fourth year I was able to be host to 
someone visiting me. 

Now that visiting is mandatory 
for membership in O.C.A., in other 
Provincial Associations, and in the 
American Camping Association, 
there is a great danger that the visit 
could become an inspection. If it 
becomes a mechanical routine chore 
that a camp must submit to, in 
order to receive the blessing of the 
Association and in order to show 
the emblem to the public, all value 
of the program is lost. We must 
keep reminding ourselves of the 
prime purpose of the visit — Com¬ 
munication — Education. 

At the present time, in addition 
to camping meetings and annual

Mandatory Standards 

Ontario Camping Association 

by Ron Johnstone 



Ron Johnstone, Director Camp White Bear, Ontario. Chair¬ 
man of Standards, Canadian Camping Association. 


At its November 1969 Board of Di¬ 
rector’s meeting, the Ontario Camping 
Association approved the implemen¬ 
tation of Mandatory Standards for Ac¬ 
credited Membership in the Associa¬ 
tion. 

The development of our Standards’ 
programme has been going on for over 
twenty-five years. Many stages have 
come and gone in our ever constant 
striving for better camping for the 
children of our Province. The road 
from ‘Desirable Camping Practices’ to 
Mandatory Standards has seen many 
people contributing their thought and 
experience to the programme. 

There is a basic attitude necessary 
to the continuing development of 
camping standards. The Association’s 
recommended Standards must be 
viewed as MINIMUM standards for 
safe camping. We must not let our¬ 
selves fall into the trap of feeling that 
we have arrived, when we are meeting 
the Standards as recommended by the 
Association. They are no more than a 
minimum guarantee, to the camping 
public of our Province, that their 
children will be safe both physically 
and mentally, in our Accredited 
Camps. 

A prime reason for our Minimum 
Standards must be to protect the chil¬ 
dren of Ontario. To ensure that they 
will have a safe camping experience 
and their physical and mental health 
will be protected at all times, while at¬ 
tending our Accredited Camps. With 
this as the main reason for Standards, 
there are however, other major con¬ 
siderations. The Standards’ Pro¬ 
gramme must continue to be educa¬ 
tional in its nature, we must strive to 
educate and uplift all aspects of our 
camping programme. With this in 
mind, the outline “Desirable Camping 
Practices’’ will still be the basis for 
Accrediting our Member Camps. The 
mutual review of the outline with an 
experienced Director in an indepth 
visit will still be the basis for main¬ 
taining our basic safe minimum level 
of camping. We urge all Camp Direc¬ 
tors and staff people who are working 
in our Camps to continue to strive to¬ 
ward better and more mature camping 
philosophies. 


There is also a very protective as¬ 
pect to our Standards’ Programme. As 
Camp operators we have a responsi¬ 
bility to the industry. We are often 
in a vulnerable position of liability in 
our work with youngsters. The liability 
we face is equated on what is the “ac¬ 
cepted common practice” within our 
profession. The adherence to the 
Camping Standards as outlined by 
your Association is YOUR protection 
that you are indeed following the ac¬ 
cepted common practice for good 
camping. This is not only protection 
for the young people of Ontario, but 


also your protection as a Camp Oper¬ 
ator within this Province. 

The Mandatory Standards’ Outline 
will now be used for the re-Accredita- 
tion of Ontario Camps. You will be 
asked to certify that you are following 
these standards and then as your Camp 
is visited, to verify that Certification. I 
would again caution any who would 
feel that we have finally arrived, we 
are still on the way. Your Standards’ 
Programme, by its very nature, will 
continue to be an ever growing and 
developing aspect of the Ontario 
Camping Association.

O.C.A. MANDATORY STANDARDS FOR RESIDENT CAMPS 

IN ORDER FOR ANY CAMP TO BE ACCREDITED, ALL OF THE FOLLOWING STANDARDS MUST BE 
COMPLIED WITH. 


Explanatory information 


A Health Licence is required by Ontario Public Health 
Act O. Reg. 518-1960 


Camp medical forms must be signed by the parent or 
guardian, and state that the person is in good physical 
condition, OR, if not in good physical condition, the limits 
of the person’s physical involvement in camping activities. 

Girls — 1 seat for each 8-10 people 

Boys — 1 seat for each 8-10 people OR 1 seat for each 

15 people if urinals are available in addition. 

Water supply must be of adequate volume, tested prior to 
the opening of camp, and re-tested regularly during the 
camp season. (Once a week). 


Director: please state information requested in columns 
alongside_ 


The MINIMUM requirement is one third of total coun¬ 
sellor staff (See definition Page 19) NEW STAFF means 
individuals not previously associated with the camp in any 
capacity. 


Numbers required: — 

Fire Brigade — Police — Hospital — Physician on call 
— Rescue Squad (where available). 

Drills to practice emergency procedures must be carried 
out during staff training 


On such inspection, any hazardous situations must be 
listed, orders given for remedial steps to be taken. Re¬ 
checked within 24 hours to see that the situation has been 
remedied. 

There must be a minimum of one staff member for each 
five campers on all trips away from camp with a minimum 
of two staff on every trip.

MANDATORY STANDARDS FOR CHILDREN’S DAY CAMPS 


The following are standards and pre¬ 
cepts which are held as being manda¬ 
tory by the Ontario Camping Associa¬ 
tion. Adherence to them determines 
the initial and continued accreditation 
of the member camp. Desirable prac¬ 
tices are listed throughout the book 
to enable the Camp Director to im¬ 
prove and maintain his own operation, 
principles and procedures. His ob¬ 
servance of them determines whether 
the Association declares him eligible 
or ineligible for accreditation. But the 
MANDATORY STANDARDS 
MUST BE CERTIFIED (by the 
Camp) AND VERIFIED (by the vis¬ 
itor) IN ORDER TO MERIT AND 
MAINTAIN ELIGIBILITY FOR 
ACCREDITATION. 

1. Tabulate staff lists as shown: 

a. Name or Payroll Number 

b. Position 

c. Birth 

d. Years Camp Staff Experience 


e. School Grade Completed 

f. New Staff 

g. Held Over 

h. Years Camper Experience 

2. Camp conforms to all pertinent lo¬ 
cal health and sanitation regula¬ 
tions, and where applicable holds 
a licence from the Ontario De¬ 
partment of Health. 

Current Licence No. 

3. The camp holds a form signed by 
the parent listing the camper’s 
physical disabilities or allergies or 
any other pertinent health infor¬ 
mation of which the camp should 
be aware. In addition, the camp 
has the following information on 
the form: 

a. Parents’ home telephone num¬ 
ber 

b. Parents’ business telephone 
number 

c. Emergency numbers, other than 
a or b

9. Emergency telephone numbers are 
posted (near telephones) for fire 
department, police, hospital and/ 
or physician on call. 

10. Staff are familiar with camp emer¬ 
gency procedures regarding acci¬ 
dents or disasters. Drills to prac¬ 
tice these procedures are carried 
out regularly. 

11. The camp director personally car¬ 
ries out safety inspections of all 
camp facilities and immediately 
takes action to remedy any hazard¬ 
ous situations. 

12. A responsible person, appropri¬ 
ately trained, is assigned to each 
ten campers on all trips away 
from the camp (exclusive of trans¬ 
portation regularly involved in 
getting campers to and from camp 
or to swimming instruction, etc.). 
The number of such persons is 
never less than two. 

13. a. The person in charge of an 

out-of-camp trip (overnight or 
longer) is at least 18 years old, 
is familiar with the territory, 
and is aware of the location 
where help can be obtained in 
case of an emergency, 
b. The person assisting on an 
overnight or longer trip is at 
least 16 years old. 

14. The camp has a registration or en¬ 
rolment form for each camper, 
providing important information 
about the child, and written con¬ 
sent of parent or guardian for 
camper’s attendance and partici¬ 
pation in activities. 

15. All road transportation equipment 
is maintained in safe operating 
condition, and meets the require¬ 
ments of the Ontario Department 
of Transport. 

16. Drivers of camp vehicles are 
properly licenced. 

17. The number of campers in trans¬ 
portation units does not exceed 
the available seating capacity of 
such units. There is at least one 
supervisory person in each vehicle 
other than the driver. 

18. The camp knows and follows all 
aspects of the Ethics and Business 
Practice of the Ontario Camping 
Association. 

19. The camp adequately provides all 
facilities and activities listed in its 
brochure. 

20. The camp has accessible telephone 
or means of immediate communi¬ 
cation with a source of aid. If 
other than telephone, state means 
of immediate communication 
used. 

21. The camp has in attendance a 
registered nurse or a qualified first 
aid person holding a St. John’s 
Ambulance or Red Cross First Aid 
Certificate.

A PAGE OF POEMS 

by 

Mary S. Edgar 


A DIRECTOR’S MEDITATION 
Silence reigns at last, no unprobed 
sound 

Disturbs the peaceful night, 

No final m u t e d whispers float 
around, 

Blacked out is every light. 

Beneath the stars 1 take an inventory; 

In solitude I ask, 

'What assets lie within the soul of 
me? 

What wisdom for the task?” 

Tomorrow keen and active they will 
wake 

To greet another day, 

Eager for its fun on hill and lake, 

Ready for come-what-may. 

Yet if one camper there should 
chance to be 

Who has some hidden need, 

If all-expectant he should turn to me 

Grant I may truly lead. 

Some shrinking, timid one may need 
to grow, 

To stand erect and sure, 

Or one who bears a burden none 
may know, 

The courage to endure. 

All will need the tonic of pure joy, 

Of laughter, light and gay, 

And most of all, for every girl and 
boy 

Friendships to light the way. 

Now 1 must go to bed and get some 
sleep 

Then fully rested rise 
With patience, wisdom, gentleness 
to meet 

The problems that arise. 


HYMN FOR THE SPACE-AGE 
(Tune: Forest Green) 

Great Spirit of the universe 
Infinity of space, 

We Earth-born mortals venture far 
Your mysteries to trace. 

Our planet looms more wonderful 
With many a beauteous land 
And boundless are the mighty works 
of Your creative hand. 

This land of ours is vast and fair, 
Shaped through the ages gone, 
Inheritors, our debt is paid 
By passing beauty on. 

Keeping our skies and waters clean 
Our forests freshly green 
Thus through the ever-circling years 
True gratitude is seen. 

None could desire a fairer land 
Nor better day and age 
To build in this our Canada 
A worthy heritage. 

Most bounteous have been Your 
gifts 

Beyond our needed share. 

Grant we may learn to freely give 
To those who poorly fare. 


POSTPONE THE VERDICT 
Have you ever known a time 
When an oldster didn't claim: 

"It isn't like it used to be! 

Youth must take the blame.” 

When you search the records 
Are you very much impressed? 
Were the Ancients, saints and an¬ 
gels, 

With special virtues blessed? 

Victorian critics muttered 

As they sniffed a pinch of snuff: 
"This country's going to the dogs! 
Youth's gone quite far enough!” 

Postpone the guilty verdict 
About the present state. 

Youth is pressing forward; 

Those dogs t vill have to wait. 


OUTDOOR BEAUTY CLINIC 
If to the rain you lift your face 
fust as the flowers do 
You'll get it very nicely washed — 
A beauty-treatment too. 

If to the wind you bare your head 
You will not need a comb, 

The breeze will swish it all about 
More gently than at home. 

If at the sky you stop to look 
You've got to stand up straight, 
Your backbone then will be erect 
For jobs that irritate. 

Beneath the blue of heaven 
You're almost sure to find 
Earth's precious healing tonic — 

A calming peace of mind.

BESOINS SPIRITUELS DANS LES CAMPS 

Conference donnee au Congres de ('Association des Camps du Quebec, 

le 21 fevrier 1970 
Pierre Cote, S.J. 


INTRODUCTION 

Souvent, vous analysez les differents 
problemes que vous rencontrez dans 
les camps, problemes sociaux de la 
jeunesse, problemes du loisir, de l’en- 
fance exceptionnelle. Vous vous in- 
formez sur les techniques nouvelles qui 
peuvent etre utilisees dans les camps, 
techniques audio-visuelles et autres. 

Maintenant, nous allons regarder en¬ 
semble une autre dimension de la vie 
dans les camps, et c’est la dimension 
spirituelle. Peut-etre le mot vous re- 
pugne-t-il au premier abord, peut-etre 
ne reveille-t-il en vous aucun aspect 
positif, et au contraire plus d’agres- 
sivite que de sympathie? Peut-etre 
vous rejoint-il dans une dimension im- 
portante de votre vie. 

BESOINS DU JEUNE 

Si vous le voulez, pour essayer de 
comprendre un peu toutes les implica¬ 
tions de cette dimension, nous allons 
d’abord nous tourner vers le jeune tel 
qu’il se presente dans les camps et 
essayer de degager rapidement quel- 
ques-uns de ses besoins les plus fon- 
damentaux. 

Tout d’abord, le jeune decouvre, en 
venant dans un camp, toute la gran¬ 
deur et la beaute de la nature. Pour 
plusieurs d’entre eux c’est la premiere 
fois qu’ils peuvent en prendre con¬ 
science et c’est la premiere fois qu’ils 
peuvent s’arreter pour contempler 
cette nature. Et vous le savez mieux 
que moi, si le miniteur ou directeur 
du camp porte une attention speciale 
a cette dimension, le jeune pourra de- 
couvrir beaucoup. 

De plus, le jeune, e l’epoque de sa 
vie oil il vient dans les camps a besoin 
de se sentir “quelqu’un”, a besoin 
qu’on porte attention a lui, qu’on ac- 
corde de l’importance a ce qu’il dit. 
Aussi i] a besoin d’aide et de support 
dans la decouverte de sa liberte. II veut 
connaitre beaucoup de choses, mais 
aussi il veut aimer. Il a besoin d’etablir 
d autres relations que celles qu’il con- 
nait avec ses parents et ses professeurs. 
Cette attention aux autres, cette decou¬ 
verte de I’autre peuvent etre plus for- 
midables encore dans un camp, car le 
climat de simplicite, de gaiete et de 
spontaneite permet d’etablir des con¬ 
tacts plus profonds avec les gens qui 
Fentourent. 

Un aspect important peut done se 


degager et du milieu de la nature oit 
le jeune se trouve plonge et du climat 
de sympathie et de simplicite ou il 
aura a vivre, et cet aspect est la gra¬ 
tuite. En effet, c’est peut-etre dans les 
camps et dans des milieux semblables 
que les personnes, jeunes ou adultes, 
peuvent experimenter le mieux la va- 
leur de la gratuite. Et le jeune, en de- 
couvrant toutes les dimensions de sa 
liberte, pourra experimenter aussi la 
grandeur de cette gratuite et la joie, 
non seulement de recevoir, mais aussi 
la joie de donner. 

Est-ce que les besoins de l’enfant 
sont tous satisfaits en repondant e son 
desir de connaitre et en lui faisant de- 
couvrir et comprendre toute la beaute 
de la nature, et en lui permettant de se 
lier tres intimement avec les personnes 
qui Fentourent? Le jeune a-t-il encore 
d’autres aspirations que celles-la? 

Et je me permets ici de repondre oui, 
mais avec des nuances. Je dis avec nu¬ 
ances, car le milieu d’ou il vient aura 
pu ou non l’eveiller a ce dont je veux 
vous parler e l’instant. En effet, encore 
aujourd’hui et dans la majorite des cas, 
le jeune vient d’un milieu familial ou 
la dimension spirituelle a de Fimpor- 
tance. Par dimension spirituelle faut-il 
entendre une pratique religieuse in¬ 
tense? Non. Faut-il entendre une foi 
en l’Eglise Catholique? Non. 

Par dimension spirituelle, je veux 
dire que, pour la majorite des parents, 
il existe a l’interieur meme de leur vie 
quotidienne ou (et) au-dela de cette 
vie quotidienne une autre dimension. 
Leurs aspirations ne seraient pas tous 
satisfaites si on ne faisait pas appel, a 
un moment ou Fautre, a un Absolu. 
Cet Absolu, bien sur, sera per$u et 
connu de differentes fa 9 ons. Pour les 
uns, ce sera l’explication de ce qui ex¬ 
iste, le premier principe, le createur 
de la nature. Pour les autres, ce sera 
“un grand bonhomme” qui dirige non 
seulement la nature, mais meme la 
destinee des personnes elles-memes. 
Pour d’autres, cet Absolu sera une 
valeur dont il faut vivre a tout prix, 
comme la paix, la fraternite, l’amitie 
etc. Pour d’autres, cet Absolu se situera 
dans les relations interpersonnelles. 
Pour d’autres enfin, cet Absolu, c’est 
Quelqu’un. Et il me semble important 
de respecter chacune de ces options. 
Mais ce que je voudrais vous signaler 
ici, c’est la presence ce cette dimension 


avec ce caractere d’Absolu. Si vous le 
voulez, nous allons l’appeler la dimen¬ 
sion spirituelle. Cette dimension est a 
la fois fortement incarnee dans 
l’homme, mais a la fois aussi elle pro- 
jete l’homme au-dela de lui-meme. Elle 
le sort de lui-meme et lui montre que 
le centre de gravie est peut-etre et en 
lui et hors de lui. Et c’est en sortant de 
soi qu’il se retrouvera le plus pro- 
fondement. 

Voila done assez brifcvement quel- 
ques uns des besoins auxquels le jeune 
veut repondre lorsqu’il vient vivre dans 
un camp. Il veut vivre en plenitude et 
intensement tant en decouvrant la na¬ 
ture, qu’en connaissant et aimant 
d’autres personnes, mais souvent aussi 
decouvertes et connaissances vecues a 
Finterieur d’une dimension spirituelle. 

ROLE DE L’EDUCATEUR 

Devant ces besoins du jeune, quel 
est votre role a vous, directeurs et 
moniteurs de camp? 

Je crois que ce role en est un d’edu- 
cateur, i.e. qui celui qui s’occupe du 
jeune doit veiller a developper toutes 
les dimensions de la personne de sorte 
que le jeune avec qui il travaille, 
s’achemine progressivement vers une 
maturite d’adulte. 

Or developper toutes les dimensions 
de la personne veut dire s’occuper a la 
fois des besoins physiques de sante, 
d’equilibre et de bien-etre, des besoins 
psychologiques et des besoins spirit- 
uels. 

Que veut dire ici s’occuper des be¬ 
soins spirituels du jeune? Comme nous 
l’avons vu tantot, le jeune vient d’un 
milieu ordinairement eveille a la di¬ 
mension spirituelle de la personne, ou 
la presence de l’Absolu est un element 
important de leur vie. Or l’educateur 
qui a a travailler avec ce jeune n’a 
pas le droit, et sous aucun pretexte, 
d’ignorer ce fait. Et meme plus il doit 
essayer de continuer le travail que les 
parents ont deja commence a la mai- 
son. Bien sur, vous allez m’objecter 
qu’il y a beaucoup de directeurs et de 
moniteurs qui ne croient pas du tout 
a cet Absolu. Peut-etre. Mais si vous 
voulez honnetement, faire un travail 
d’educateurs, vous n’avez pas le droit 
d’ignorer volontairement une dimen¬ 
sion importante de la personne, dimen¬ 
sion que plusieurs reconnaissent 
comme etant encore valables. 

Et selon le degre de votre croyance 


12 



Photo — Colonie de Vacances des Greves, Inc. 


a cet Absolu, il vous sera demande 
davantage, i.e. si nous n’avez aucune 
croyance a cet Absolu, il vous faut au 
moins respecter une option differente 
de la votre, sans la mepriser et sans 
denigrer contre elle, sans en rire et 
sans la ridiculiser. Si vous y croyez un 
peu, il vous faudra deja faire plus, et 
aider le jeune a decouvrir avec vous 
cette dimension de la personne. Enfin, 
si vous y croyez beaucoup et que cet 
Absolu est une Presence dans votre vie, 
alors il vous fardra faire partage cette 
presence et travailler de telle sorte que 
cet Absolu devicnne aussi un Presence 
pour la jeune. 

Comme vous pouvez le constater, la 
premiere condition essentielle pour 
qu’un travail d’education puisse se 
faire, c'est le respect integral et des 
personnes qui nous entourent et des 
options des autres personnes, meme si 
ces options ne cadrent pas avec nos 
convictions. Et ce respect doit se mani- 
fester autant de la part d’un directeur 
de camp vis-a-vis les options de ses 
moniteurs pour ne leur demander que 
ce qu’ils peuvent donner, et vis-a-vis 
scs campeurs pour ne pas leur imposer 
un horaire et une fagon de vivre con- 


traire a l’option du milieu dont ils sont 
issus, autant des moniteurs vis-a-vis 
des jeunes avec qui ils travaillent et 
vis-a-vis Pesprit du camp ou ils tra¬ 
vaillent. 

Ce n’est que dans un tel climat 
d’acceptation et de respect de l’autre 
que le vrai travail l’education pourra 
se realiser. 

APPLICATIONS CONCRETES 

Comment vivre tout cela, concrete- 
ment dans un camp? Ici, ma reponse 
sera breve, car c’est a vous a le de¬ 
couvrir. En effet, une fois admises 
toutes les valeurs que nous voulons 
vivre et faire vivre dans un camp, c’est 
aux directeurs et aux moniteurs de 
camp a voir comment incarner ces va- 
lcurs. Et vous le savez bien, il n’y a 
pas de formules magiques. 

Est-ce que cela voudra dire qu’il 
faut imposer la messe quotidienne ou 
hebdomadaire? Peut-etre qui oui, peut- 
etre que non. L’integration de la di¬ 
mension spirituelle dans le camp ne se 
fera pas d'abord en imposant un cadre 
de l'exterieur pour forcer l’expression 
de cette dimension, mais davantage par 
une attention a revolution des per¬ 
sonnes qui vivent au camp, attention 


qui conduira a expliciter et a exprimer 
plus specialement cette dimension 
spirituelle. Mais encore la, si on sort 
de cadres bien precis et securisants, il 
faudra faire beaucoup appel a l’imagi- 
nation et surtout, saisir les occasions 
ou cette dimension spirituelle a besoin 
de s'exprimer et d'etre explicitee pour 
elle-meme. 

Bien que moins rassurante, je crois 
que cette fa?on de porter attention et 
de respecter la dimension spirituelle 
de sa vie portera des fruits beaucoup 
plus grands et engagera davantage 
aussi toute la vie de ceux qui auront a 
y travailler. 

CONCLUSION 

En terminant, je voudrais vous dire 
encore une fois a quel point le respect 
des personnes qui nous entourent et 
de leurs options est important. Dans 
un camp, le contact prolongc avec la 
nature eveillera assez spontanement 
plusieurs a une dimension spirituelle. 
Bien plus encore, la rencontre veritable 
d’autres personnes suscitera peut-etre 
le desir et le besoin de rencontrer la 
Personne par excellence, l'Absolu, le 
Seigneur.

BADGES AND AWARDS: 
A POSITIVE VIEWPOINT 


Competition and measuring ones 
progress are essential to the growth 
and development of every individ¬ 
ual. Awards and badges ean be the 
greatest motivating factor available 
to young people. National, provin¬ 
cial or camp tests based upon an 
individuals progress in activities 
encourage the development of skills. 
Recently, educational institutions 
have changed from promotion of 
students by single grade level to pro¬ 
motion at the individual subject 
level. Such a scheme has been used 
in camps for many years and with 
great success. An award or badge 
given for achievement at each step 
in learning, permits the camper to 
proceed at his own rate and be at 
a variety of stages in the total pro¬ 
gram. Opportunities to motivate 
campers in developing activity skills 
are being ignored by those camps 
who eliminate badges and graded 
levels of achievement. 

When award objectives are estab¬ 
lished, the position of the camper 
must be the first to be considered. 
Development of a valid program is 
camper-centered. Although young 
people present many challenges to 
the adults of today, they also experi¬ 
ence, in turn, a strong need to be 
challenged. Campers need to know 
where they stand in relation to their 
peers and the adults with whom 
they are involved. Campers enjoy 
helping each other yet may be re¬ 
luctant when they lack knowledge 
of their own capabilities. Recogniz¬ 
ing their skill level through the pass¬ 
ing of specific awards gives campers 
an indication of their ability. 
Graded skill levels provide a chal¬ 
lenge through which campers are 
motivated to adventure and to 
(strive for) further knowledge. 

Every individual needs to possess 
a sense of self-worth. Positive com¬ 
parative evaluation with others can 
reinforce ones self-esteem. The ad¬ 
vantages of award levels in fulfilling 
this sense of worth are evident at a 
camp where various levels of pro¬ 
gress can exist in different camp 
skills. These levels arc clear-cut and 
obvious to each camper. The master 


by Jocelyn Palm 
Executive Secretary 
Royal Life-Saving Society, Toronto 


canoeist may be a crew member in 
a sailboat but is encouraged by 
others who have achieved the high¬ 
est sailing awards. This camper has, 
at the same time, a knowledge that 
he is more skilled in canoeing. 

When campers find themselves at 
various levels of proficiency in camp 
activities they may more readily ac¬ 
cept their limitations in other areas. 
This reality, when accepted and un¬ 
derstood, assists the camper to ef¬ 
ficiently utilize his capabilities and 
acquired skills. 

Skill development may prove to 
be a very subtle process. This fact is 
particularly evident in learning to 
swim where the learner may not feel 
he has achieved a great deal during 
certain phases of the learning pro¬ 
cess. Through the attainment of a 
badge, the mastery of some skill is 
confirmed to him. 

Upon earning an award at a cer¬ 
tain level the camper has a specific 
basis upon which to seek further as¬ 
sistance from others. The opportun¬ 
ity for mutual understanding and 
guidance is provided. 

Skills are the basis upon which 
camps attempt to ensure the safety 
of their campers. For example, ef¬ 
ficiency in specific swimming and 
canoeing skills is necessary for a 
camper to go on a canoe trip or be 
permitted to travel through white 
water. A camper who knows he pos¬ 
sesses these skills may find satisfac¬ 
tion and challenge in employing the 
principles he has mastered. A camp¬ 
er who is unsure of himself may 
experience fear rather than recog¬ 
nizing an attainable goal. 

Most young people establish a 
competitive relationship with their 
peers. To be useful, the competition 
must motivate others to seek an 
equal or superior level of skill. 
Awards and badges are the visible 
signs of this achievement and the 
evidence of success. 

Badges and awards are often the 
basis upon which the parent gives 
recognition to the camper. Although 
this fact is criticized by some, a 
child is able to explain to his parents 
what level of skill he has achieved 


through the requirements of the 
award. Many disciplines learned at 
camp are only practised at camp; 
therefore, the parent may not have 
an opportunity to investigate what 
the camper has learned. Learning is 
more enjoyble when it can be shared 
by the camper and his parent. 
Badges indicate the results of learn¬ 
ing. Parents want to know what 
their children are doing; although 
they may be unfamiliar with the 
specific skills which have been mas¬ 
tered in gaining a badge, the badge 
itself is the camper's tangible con¬ 
firmation of achievement. 

Recorded evidence of campers’ 
skill level is essential to the camp 
director. He uses this information 
to determine and organize the ac¬ 
tivities which lie may offer to his 
campers and staff. A prospective 
staff member may claim to have all 
the required safety skills in riflery 
and aquatics, but without credentials 
to prove his capabilities the camp 
director should be reluctant to hire 
such an individual. The legal im¬ 
plications in hiring staff without 
current qualifications are of the ut¬ 
most significance. Most camps ob¬ 
tain their senior personnel through 
the ranks of their own organization. 
Then, is it not fair to provide the 
opportunity for campers to achieve 
recognized awards while they are 
campers? 

The camp director may effective¬ 
ly use award levels in order to or¬ 
ganize camp program, to determine 
what challenges he can safely place 
before his campers and to regulate 
the privileges he will permit staff 
and campers. In order to encourage 
a camper to continue his association 
with his camp, the earning of badges 
and awards can be very important. 

Camping skills and activities pro¬ 
vide experiences for a camper’s fu¬ 
ture recreational pursuits. The camp 
program emphasizing badges and 
awards offers an environment for 
the camper to progress at his ability 
level and to continue to do so once 
he leaves camp. Thus, the contrib¬ 
ution of badges and awards can be 
a very positive influence to the ma¬ 
turing of today’s youth. 


14 


BADGES AND AWARDS: 
A NEGATIVE VIEWPOINT 


Human beings have a basic thirst 
for knowledge which begins at birth 
and continues in many ways 
throughout the rest of their adult 
lives. Education has become the fa¬ 
cilitator of learning in our world 
community and also enables us to 
take our place in society as workers 
in many walks of life. Unfortunate¬ 
ly, the world has become a place 
where competition and power in¬ 
fluence the personality of society 
and also the individuals who make 
up society. The system of merit 
badges and achievement awards 
which instills a competitive drive 
within the individual has done a 
great deal for prosperity in our busi¬ 
ness and industry but little for the 
learning process which should be 
the basis of our educational system. 
The learning process in our educa¬ 
tional system has been smudged by 
our training process. 

Camp is one of our most basic 
institutions for learning, one which 
provides us with the knowledge of 
people, a skill in my opinion we 
have neglected somewhat, and our 
society shows it. Camp should be a 
place where there is no system of 
badges and awards. Competition 
should exist, but it should be for the 
benefit of oneself and not for the 
idle conversation of a camper’s par¬ 
ent such as has been the case with 
our beloved report cards. The com¬ 
petitive system is incorporated into 
every facet of our society not just 
here but all over the world. 

Did you ever stop and think what 
the competitive system has done to 
us? Competition has caused wars, 
bitterness, racial hatred, people who 
go hungry, and it has robbed the 
individual of his right to personal 
growth and development. Most of 
all, competition has robbed use of the 
opportunity to be ourselves. I am 
not advocating overthrow of the 
business world, but what I am saying 
is that competition and its facili¬ 
tators, badges and awards, be re¬ 
moved from our educational insti¬ 
tutions and most of all our summer 
camps. 

Badges and awards, in my opin¬ 
ion, are detrimental to the purpose 
of a camp which is, I hope, to have 
fun within a learning experience. If 
you remove badges and awards from 
a camp setting you will cause less 


by John H. Walker 
Springfield College and 
Kilcoo Camp 

friction between cabin and camper 
and also the staff, thus resulting in a 
more harmonious camp. Badges and 
awards have for so long stifled the 
individual that learning becomes 
secondary to winning and out-doing 
the other guy. The prime purpose 
of a badge has been to measure one’s 
ability in society. The achievement 
of a badge or award overshadows 
the amount of learning which takes 
place and chips away humaneness, 
which, in turn, corrupts the individ¬ 
ual’s personality and makes him 
cold, and a product of the system. 

Camp is a place where human re¬ 
lations play a big part in the daily 
life of a camper. If badges and 
awards and attainment of those 
awards pressure the child, then con¬ 
flicts within himself and others 
arise. 

The individual becomes frus¬ 
trated at failing. Actually failing is 
something not to be ashamed of, but 
is rather, a learning experience 
which everyone experiences at some 
time in his life. The fault of our 
system is that we measure every¬ 
thing by the number of badges a 
person has, or the number of de¬ 
grees. and so on, throughout the 
structure. Badges and awards indi¬ 
cate the results of learning because 
our system dictates that in order for 
a person to be a success in life, he 
must show society in some way that 
he has achieved status. Learning 
cannot be measured properly by an 
award. An individual could attain 
all the badges and awards in the 
world yet he might not have learned 
as much as the person next to him 
at the canoe dock or in classroom. 
A successful life and pursuit of hap¬ 
piness should be the motivating fac¬ 
tor in an individual, not the pursuit 
of happiness through the badge or 
award in a forced learning situation. 
Being a total human being is a shar¬ 
ing experience between people; 
badges and awards certainly do not 
follow along those lines. The pres¬ 
ent system of standards at camp is 
not all bad, but it should be modi¬ 
fied to include more humanitarian 
ideals which I hope camping, edu¬ 
cation and the outdoors is all about. 
Camp supplies a need which our 
schools tend to neglect. The skills 
we need are the people skills. Man 


has solved the problem of reaching 
the moon, but everywhere we must 
devote ourselves to solving the hu¬ 
man problem, our most basic and 
most worthy. 

In order to change our system of 
badges and awards we must change 
our method of grading in our schools 
and also our standards of achieve¬ 
ment. Our grading and award sys¬ 
tem should be commensurate with 
our new concepts of education 
where the individual proceeds at his 
or her own speed, and the self- 
concept and confidence is enhanced 
in the individual. A major fault of 
grading and awarding is that we dis¬ 
illusion so many young people who 
become hung up on passing and fail¬ 
ing with little learning and fun. It 
is something we all should think 
about. Maybe all those people who 
can t smile or laugh will someday 
know what being happy is all about. 

My solution to the problem of 
abolition of badges and awards 
would be to create a system whereby 
an individual will be able to evalu¬ 
ate himself as a person who has 
grown from his experience, or an in¬ 
dividual who is aware of his learn¬ 
ing. Also I think there must be a 
measure of ones ability, but I be¬ 
lieve it starts with the individual 
and his peers and not with a test or 
examination. 

In an activity, learning should be 
a progression, but the instructor is 
the key to proficient learning 
as is the case with swimming. If the 
instructor really cares about his 
teaching he will decide whether or 
not his campers are learning what 
they are being taught. In turn, the 
campers will show and use what 
they have learned instead of always 
being tested and pressured. It is 
often the weak instructor who re¬ 
lies on tests to accomplish what he 
himself can not do. 

Learning a skill in camp should 
be a progression of learned material 
which is simultaneous with the 
child’s increasing ability, and hence 
an experience from which a child 
grows to maturity. However, badges 
and awards do serve a purpose for 
those who feel insecure enough in 
the learning process to warrant a 
conditioned response which is what 
a badge or award is in human terms.

A Place in History for 
Ontario Camping 


A ceremony took place at Trent 
University, Peterborough last fall. 
On October 22 nd, the archives col¬ 
lected by the Ontario Camping As¬ 
sociation were presented by past 
president, John Latimer to the Trent 
archival collection of Canadiana. 
These were accepted by Dr. T. H. B. 
Symonds, president of the Univer¬ 
sity. 

Some thirty members of the On¬ 
tario Camping Association motored 
to Trent through the first autumn 
snowstorm. Following the ceremony 
in the University’s beautiful new li¬ 
brary, lunch was served in the Great 
Hall. To enliven the proceedings, 
a French play was put on by die 
students. Later the Ontario Camp¬ 
ing Association members were taken 
on a tour of the University and the 
day ended with a tea party at Dr. 
Bruno Morawetz’ farm a short dis¬ 
tance up the Otonobee River. 

This occasion marked six years 
of effort by the archives committee 
of the O.C.A. under the successive 
chairmanships of Mrs. Adele Ebbs, 
Miss Margaret Govan and Dr. Mary 
North way. During this period, rec¬ 
ords from many individual camps 
and of the Association had been col¬ 
lected, stored and catalogued at the 
O.C.A. office by Mrs. Shirley Hall. 
Much important material — early 
brochures, photographs, pro¬ 
grammes and schedules, films, fi¬ 
nancial accounts, diaries, and taped 
interviews of prominent camp per¬ 
sonalities had been received and 
used by students and others for stud¬ 
ies. Now a duplicate file of these is 
kept at the camping office and 
the invaluable, original documents 
stored in Trents safe keeping as a 
permanent part of the Canadian 
record. 

Other provincial associations may 
wish to collect their own archives 
and eventually transfer these to a 
permanent collection. They may 
first ask the question we did, u Why 


by Mary L. Northway 
Chairman, Archives Committee 


archives?”. A fine answer was given 
to us by Mr. J. D. P. Martin, li¬ 
brarian at Trent as follows: 

“A historian said recently that a 
community which does not know its 
own history is like a man who has 
lost his memory. The same is true 
of an institution, organization, or 
association which has failed to pre¬ 
serve the documents that record 
its traditions and achievements. 
Knowledge of its origin and devel¬ 
opment provides an association with 
a sense of historic purpose which 
gives it direction for the future. An 
archives serves as an association’s 
‘memory’ of its own historical evo¬ 
lution. 

“It is the function of an archives 
to collect, arrange, store and retrieve 
the official and unofficial records 
relating to an association’s develop¬ 
ment, and to provide reference serv¬ 
ices to users of the collection. Sam¬ 
ples of the kind of records which 
should be collected are as follows: 
Legal documents, minute books (of 
the association and all its commit¬ 
tees with supporting documents 
such as reports and letters), official 
correspondence, accounting records, 
annual reports, camp records, draw¬ 
ings and plans, etc., records relating 
to personnel, personal papers relat¬ 
ing to people who have been active 
in the camping movement (diaries, 
journals, correspondence, etc.), 
photographs, and miscellaneous pa¬ 
pers (essays, lectures, etc.) which 
can throw light on the association or 
the camping movement. 

“The archives of a camping asso¬ 
ciation is more than simply a record 
of its own historic past. It is also a 
repository of material relating to an 
important aspect of social history. 
By stimulating scholarly interest in 
its contents it can be expected to 
make a major contribution to the 
history of the whole community.” 

Another question asked was, 


“what to collect?”. The answer was, 
“everything”. “Let the archivist de¬ 
cide what is not important.” It was 
also emphasized that material com¬ 
ing in should not be sorted by ama¬ 
teurs, but stored in its original pack¬ 
ages and catalogued from these. 

Finally the question will be 
raised, “but this costs money?”. So 
it does — a part-time secretary who 
is vitally interested is essential, so 
is storage space, card catalogues and 
filing cabinets. (A great deal of vol¬ 
untary work on the part of an en¬ 
thusiastic committee is of course the 
core of such a project.) Ontario was 
fortunate because the writers of The 
Camp Counselors Book (the manu¬ 
script of which is now part of the 
Trent archives) turned over the roy¬ 
alties to the Association for such a 
purpose. However, the costs were 
not great and other associations, if 
they become interested in archives, 
could certainly find funds. 

So what comes out of such a col¬ 
lection? Do they just collect dust? 
No indeed. Camp people may use 
them to study the history of Ontario 
camping, or of a camp, or for biog¬ 
raphies of pioneer campers. Social 
scientists may consult them to inves¬ 
tigate changes in programmes, phil¬ 
osophies or the camp population — 
economists may be interested in the 
costs and fees, sources of financing. 
Educationalists may investigate pro¬ 
cedures that had their origins in 
camping situations. Conservationists 
may well want access to them; and 
so on. 

Let’s remember “archives are to 
groups, as memory is to the individ¬ 
ual. Knowledge of the past enlight¬ 
ens our understanding of the pres¬ 
ent and as a flashlight illumines 
trails to the future”. 

“The record of today, becomes 
the archive of tomorrow.” Begin col¬ 
lecting now — not only the old, 
but current material that will be¬ 
come history in the future.

Photo by Ontario Department of Tourism and Information

YOUTH AND DRUGS 

A paper presented to The Society of Camp Directors 
on April 9th, 1970 


As camp directors our primary con¬ 
cern is with youth. It is important to 
realize that the youth of 1970 is not 
the youth of 1965. It would be dif¬ 
ficult to find an instance where change 
has been so rapid and so profound as 
in the growth of the present drug cul¬ 
ture. 

The generation gap is nothing new. 
There always has been a generation 
gap and the generation gap has always 
been closed when the young reached 
mature years. Today, we also have a 
generation gap, but in addition to this 
we have a deep gulf and that which 
separates the two sides of the gulf is 
the use of drugs. On one side of the 
gulf are the drug takers and on the 
other side are the adults and the youth 
who are not on drugs. The generation 
gap exists side by side with the gulf. 
The generation gap will be closed 
when our conservative youth becomes 
older, but the gulf will persist and 
those on the other side will become 
more numerous. 

Who are the persons on the other 
side of the gulf? Among them are our 
campers and counsellors, our high 
school and university students; they 
are our sons and daughters. They are 
excellent young boys and girls and just 
because they have joined the drug cul¬ 
ture we must not despair over them. 

I must confess to you that the spec¬ 
tre of a drug using youth haunted me 
terribly a few years ago. I remember 
the panic which came over me when 
I imagined my counsellors or campers 
stealthily smoking pot behind the craft 
area. I have lost some of this panic, 
because I have tried to analyze the 
drug phenomenon and to understand 
something about it. 

It is the purpose of my paper to 
explore with you THEIR side of the 


by Bruno Morawetz, Ph.D. 


drug question and to make us, older 
folk, understand their motives and 
their rationale. Since I have not taken 
any drugs, I must depend on what I 
have read and on what I have been 
told. 

Before going any further I must 
point to a qualification which is al¬ 
ready well understood, especially by 
your responsible young drug users. 
Since they know a great deal more 
about drugs than we do, it is com¬ 
forting to know, that they too draw a 
sharp line between the mild psyche¬ 
delic drugs like Marijuana and LSD 
on the one hand, and the dangerous 
drugs like heroin and speed. Their 
thinking seems to be that there are 
no dangers in smoking marijuana or 
hashish and that the occasional LSD 
trip is dangerous only in the case of 
emotionally unstable persons, but for 
others well worth the risk. 

The responsible drug users are dis¬ 
mayed by the irresponsible use of 
heroin and speed, but they are equally 
dismayed at the paranoic attitude of 
their elders towards the psychedelic 
(mind-manifesting) drugs. If the drug 
issue is to be resolved the YOUNG 
will have to regulate it. I have no 
doubt that within a few years proper 
information and adequate laws will 
be forthcoming. 

If we are going to play our part as 
leaders of youth, we should understand 
why so many of our young are taking 
drugs. Let us therefore pretend that 
we are looking at our world with the 
eyes of a seventeen-year-old. 

Our young eyes would see a world 
which does not look too appealing. 
They would see a world in which man¬ 
kind wages war upon its own species, 
and on every other living species. A 
world, in which a lethal carpet of 
concrete and metal covers the soft 


body of the earth. A world of artificial 
scarcities when millions are in desper¬ 
ate need of food. A world where ma¬ 
terial values are glorified and spiritual 
values degraded. A world of polluted 
air, polluted rivers and oceans so that 
men can grow rich in material things 
they do not need. A world in which 
the mass media are monopolized for 
the sake of economic gain. A world in 
which nudity and sex are exploited for 
commercial purposes. A world in 
which adults fill jobs they do not be¬ 
lieve in, a world of spiritual emptiness 
which drives adults to alcohol and 
and illicit sex, to nervous breakdowns 
and mental illness. A world which has 
seen one mushroom cloud and is pre¬ 
paring for more of them. A world 
(and this is the most horrible of all 
discoveries) in which human beings 
are no longer needed. We live in a 
world where some of the best brains 
devote themselves to the problem of 
how to keep idle millions busy and, 
hopefully, sane. 

I do not think that I have falsified 
the picture as it meets the eye of the 
seventeen-year-old. You and I do not 
like this picture any more than they 
do, but most of us here are not stand¬ 
ing at the threshold of this world. 
Many of us are “over the hill” and 
console ourselves with that thought. 

Many of the sensitive and idealistic 
teenagers look at this world and have 
no desire to join it. They feel that 
they wish to create for themselves a 
new and different world, a world in 
which spiritual values override mate¬ 
rial ones. 

I wish to submit that the revolution 
we are witnessing is a spiritual revolu¬ 
tion, one in which drugs play only a 
certain part. The revolution is not re¬ 
stricted to Toronto or Ontario. It is 


19 



taking place in every province in Can¬ 
ada, in every state of the U.S., in 
France, Germany, Holland, Scandi¬ 
navia, in short it is taking place in 
every industrialized society. We are 
witnessing the results of the computer 
revolution and we must learn to see 
it in its proper global perspective. 

History may be the result of human 
decisions, but when millions of human 
decisions are added up, history be¬ 
comes a steamroller that no individ¬ 
ual can stop. It is unfortunate that 
some of the young blame their elders 
for the world as it is today. We elders 
do not like it any more than they do. 
Perhaps we need to make this clear 
to them instead of defending our kind 
of world with mulish stubbornness. 

The young protest against the im¬ 
personal nature of city life, against a 
consumer oriented society, against 
canned mass entertainment, against a 
work-ethic which no longer serves a 
computerized society; they protest 
against the spectacle of men becoming 
machines. 

They realize that the steamroller of 
history cannot be halted and yet they 
want to go on living. The young are 
therefore creating their own kind of 
life. If you were familiar with what 
took place at Woodstock, N.Y. and 
what may take place in Ontario this 
summer, you will realize that there is 


developing a mass movement, the like 
of which has not been seen for cen¬ 
turies. They are withdrawing into a 
world of their own, bound together 
by rock music, drugs and a sense of 
community. Perhaps they are right in 
sensing that our civilization is on a col¬ 
lision course. Are we going to pretend 
that it will all blow over in a couple 
of years or are we going to try to un¬ 
derstand them and re-establish com¬ 
munication with them? We are not 
communicating if we merely tell them 
what fools they are. Perhaps we can 
learn something from them as they 
might benefit from our wisdom and 
experience. We yearn for a return to 
the good old days. How realistic is 
this? 

Have we asked ourselves in all hon¬ 
esty why we object to their beards and 
long hair, their sexual freedom, their 
outlandish clothing or their desire to 
bask in the sun and return to the land? 

The other night I attended a most 
instructive lecture at Trent University. 
Prof. Bagnani of the Department of 
Classics illustrated by means of slides 
the changes in hair and beard styles 
through the centuries. He showed the 
ages in which Jesus was represented 
cleanshaven and the change to a beard 
in the 4th century. He showed the 
cleanshaven Romans and the introduc¬ 
tion of beards. Beards were adopted 


by the popes and later discarded. 
Kings often set the pattern for beard 
and hair styles. Why do we object to 
hair styles which we find fully accept¬ 
able in saints, popes, kings or phil¬ 
osophers? Does our revulsion against 
hair styles, fashions and sexual free¬ 
dom betray a tinge of jealousy or a 
mournful acknowledgment of our fad¬ 
ing youthfulness? This is a question 
we should ask ourselves in all honesty. 

Up to this point I have traced the 
reasons why the youth are forming a 
culture of their own. I would like to 
examine now what the High Priests of 
Psychedelia are preaching. The men I 
have in mind are Aldous Huxley, Tim¬ 
othy Leary and Alan W. Watts. 

Some fifteen years ago Huxley pub¬ 
lished the now famous book The 
Doors of Perception. He took the title 
from a sentence in William Blake 
which read somewhat as follows, “If 
the doors of perception were opened 
all things would appear to us as they 
really are*’. William Blake knew that 
our sense organs screen out the rich 
variety of the sensory world. Our con¬ 
sciousness seems to select for its at¬ 
tention only those things which seem 
important. We know that children ex¬ 
perience a much richer world than we 
do. They are not yet conditioned to 
select the narrow range of things 
which are important for survival. As

X 


20 









we grow older we see less and less 
richly. We cut out sounds and sights 
and smells if they are not immediately 
important. 

Huxley took mescalin and the 
world presented itself to him in its 
tremendous wealth of vibrant colour, 
shimmering with light and pulsating 
with life. Mescalin is a substance 
found in the peyote cactus and has 
been used by Mexicans in religious 
ceremonies for many centuries. It has 
the effect which the bread and wine 
of the communion feast had for early 
Christians. 

Huxley recognized that mescalin 
could restore to us the original spirit¬ 
ual awareness which civilized man has 
gradually lost. It enabled him to 
heighten his spiritual awareness and 
to come into communion once again 
with the spiritual forces permeating 
the universe. We civilized men have 
heard of the revelations of the great 
mystics, St. John, St. Paul, Dante, 
Blake and others who report visions of 
beautiful sights or blinding lights, but 
we tend to write them off just because 
we can’t share their experiences. 

It can hardly be denied that the aim 
of religion is to alter one’s conscious¬ 
ness. Everything done in worship, 
from incense to music is designed to 
alter the consciousness of the wor¬ 
shipper. Huxley and Leary urge us to 
remove from our senses the veil which 
prevents us from seeing the created 
world in all its beauty and richness. 
Nature has provided edible plants 
which restore to us our full vision. 
More recently, the active ingredients 
in these plants have been synthesized 
in the lab and are available to those 
who wish to see what the mystics and 
seers speak about. Men have always 
strained to reach a state of ecstasy, 
either through prayer or fasting or 
flagellation or through eating certain 
foods or smoking certain herbs. The 
Buddhists and Hindus founded their 
religious symbols and doctrines under 
the influence of Indian Hemp, now 
called marijuana and hashish. It is no 
wonder that our drug culture leans 
toward Indian Religion because their 
symbolism and their teachings make 
sense when you can duplicate their 
experience with psychedelic drugs. 
Men have always used the greatest 
ingenuity to broaden and deepen their 
experience of the world. They have 
invented telescopes to see the distant 
galaxies. They have invented micro¬ 
scopes to see the tiny organisms inac¬ 
cessible to the naked eye. They have 
invented instruments for hearing in¬ 
audible sounds and now they have dis¬ 
covered substances which allow us to 
experience the spiritual world. Are we 
entitled to say to the micro-biologist 


“because you can not see the tiny or¬ 
ganisms except by artificial means, 
what you are seeing is not real”? Are 
we entitled to say to the mescaline 
user “because you use an unusual sub¬ 
stance, what you see under its in¬ 
fluence is not real”? Galileo was threat¬ 
ened with death not to reveal what 
he saw through the telescope, Leary 
is in jail for telling us that psychedelic 
drugs can expand our consciousness. 

Ever since Einstein, everyone knows 
that matter is basically energy. Leary 
tells us that with psychedelic drugs we 
can become conscious of the very en¬ 
ergy which constitutes the universe. 

He distinguishes seven levels of en¬ 
ergy, each of which is studied by a 
separate science. Level 1 is the elec¬ 
tron studied by physics and astro¬ 
physics. With the drug LSD one can 
arouse an atomic energy conscious¬ 
ness, in which one experiences the 
white light which blinded St. Paul on 
the Road to Damascus. 

Level 2 are the DNA molecules 
which programme the growth and de¬ 
velopment of the organism. They are 
studied by Biochemistry and can be 
directly experienced at the Cellular 
energy consciousness level induced by 
Peyote, Psilocybin and Yage. 

Level 3 are the automatic nerve 
plexes studied by physiology, and ex¬ 
perienced at the Somatic energy con¬ 
sciousness level with Hashish or MDA. 

Level 4 is the brain — studied by 
neurology and experienced in sensory 
energy consciousness with the aid of 
marijuana. 

There are three more levels reach¬ 
ing down to the lowest form of con¬ 
sciousness, the void which is below 
emotional stupor and is attained by 
poisons or substances like heroin. 

Most of us operate at level 3, the 
mental-social energy consciousness 
studied by psychology. 

Many of our religions urge us to 
raise ourselves above the everyday 
level of consciousness, and Buddhism 
is the one religion which transports its 
adherents to the highest level of con¬ 
sciousness. To us, who are used to 
dealing with verbal symbols, the in¬ 
sights of the Buddhists seem like so 
much gobblygook, but we are urged 
by the High Priests of psychedelia to 
take a voyage to the higher levels. To 
Huxley, Watts and Leary the taking 
of psychedelic drugs is not just a mat¬ 
ter of cheap kicks. On the contrary it 
is a serious, and at times perilous road, 
to religious experience and insight. 
They tell us, that after such a voyage 
a person is never the same. It is like 
the experience of all those who are re¬ 
born into a new life. After such an 
experience the words of Jesus become 
meaningful “Behold the birds of the 


air and the lilies of the field, they 
neither toil nor spin”. The twice-born 
individual can not share our concern 
for clothes, delicacies, furnishings and 
the trappings of civilized life. He drops 
out of that kind of life. Instead, he 
looks for a close community, for the 
simple things in life and for a return 
to nature. He is the “noble savage” of 
the twentieth century. He will spend 
whatever time is necessary to earn the 
necessities of life. But in his spare 
time he will explore the inner space of 
his consciousness. To him, this is the 
answer to the problem of leisure. To 
him this is a healthier pastime than 
sitting in a large arena clapping or 
booing and doing the same thing in 
front of the T.V. screen. 

It has been predicted that drugs will 
be the religion of the twenty first cen¬ 
tury. There is no denying that the drug 
culture has already taken on the as¬ 
pect of a religious movement. It has 
its own language, its own music, its 
own dress, its underground press, its 
own rituals and its places of congre¬ 
gation. It is a turning away from the 
world and an affirmation of spiritual 
over material values. When the history 
of this movement is written it will have 
its own saints and martyrs, of whom 
Leary will certainly be one. We who 
persecute them are the Pharisees, the 
righteous ones who take it on our¬ 
selves to jail them. 

What is their attitude toward the 
Pharisees? They look at their whisky 
drinking and beer guzzling elders and 
they pity them. They ask themselves, 
why take a depressive drug like alcohol 
which makes so many belligerent when 
you can take a peaceable drug like 
marijuana? Why dull one’s sensitivity 
with alcohol? Why not have it height¬ 
ened with marijuana? They look into 
their parents’ medicine chests and 
watch them swallow tranquillizers and 
pep-pills and they ask, if they can alter 
their consciousness, why can we not 
alter ours? 

If they are told that drugs are dan¬ 
gerous, they point to the dangers of 
cigarettes, alcohol, birth-control pills. 
If they are told that they are taking 
undue chances and unknown risks, 
they point to the explorers and scien¬ 
tists who risked their lives to conquer 
new worlds and new vistas. The men 
who sailed the oceans in flimsy crafts 
or explored the mighty rivers of our 
North would have been much safer in 
their beds. I am sure their mothers told 
them this! 

I am not defending those youngsters 
who take drugs just for kicks. But I 
am trying to understand why so many 
of our intelligent and sensitive young 
men and women join in the drug cul¬ 
ture. I am led to believe, that many of 


21 



them feel like the Pilgrim Fathers who 
wanted to remove themselves from a 
society they considered wicked. Where 
can our young go if they wish to with¬ 
draw peaceably? Since they can not 
flee physically, they remove them¬ 
selves physchologically. They resent 
being computerized; they resent being 
processed in sausage machine univer¬ 
sities; they resent bombardment by 
T.V. advertisers; they resent canned 
entertainment. 

If we are honest with ourselves, we 
too resent our present mode of life. 
We too are disturbed about pollution, 
depersonalization, loose sexual morals, 
parental neglect, family break-ups, 
commercialized sex, lack of pride in 
workmanship, postal delays, traffic tie- 
ups. We too ask “What is the world 
coming to? How long can it keep go¬ 
ing? Are we on a collision course”? 
We can not blame the drug culture for 
the ills of industrialization. Can we 
blame them for wanting to get off the 
bus? In passing judgment on them, are 
we not passing judgment on ourselves? 

Most of us have been on the bus 
for a long time and we are too old to 
get off. We see the end of the road 
ahead of us and console ourselves that 
we will soon be home. Even if we 
could, we would not know how to 
get off the bus. For this reason, most 
of us defend our ways, though we 
ourselves do not really believe in them. 
We are fighting a rear-guard action 
and are likely to lose it. They will con¬ 
vert us, as they have converted us with 
sideburns, miniskirts, psychedelic art 
and pop music. Our laws will change 
and when this Society meets again in 
1990 the smells of marijuana cigarettes 
may well waft through this room. If 
they disregard our present laws, they 
defend themselves by pointing to much 
greater crimes which go unpunished. 
Is a drag on a weed really more crim¬ 
inal than polluting everyone’s air and 
water? 

The purpose of my talk is to re¬ 
move the paranoid fear and revulsion 
which we all have at the sound of 
“drug’’ or “dope”. We must look at the 
problem in an intelligent and balanced 
manner. 

If we are to have a future, our hope 
must lie in the young. Our young are 
as honest and moral as we are, if not 
more so. If we fail to understand 
them, we can not communicate with 
them. If we do not communicate with 
them, we can not add our insights and 
experience to mould the future which 
hopefully belongs to us both. 

Copyright: The Society of Camp Directors 
and Bruno Morawetz, Ph.D., April 9th, 1970. 
Permission to reproduce all or part of this 
paper may be obtained by writing to The 
Secretary, The Society of Camp Directors, 
Box 173, Postal Station ‘S', Toronto 20, On¬ 
tario, Canada. 


TO WHOM TRIBUTE IS DUE 
Gertrude Evelyn Moore 

It was with deep regret that we 
heard of the passing of one of Can¬ 
ada s pioneer leaders in girls' camp¬ 
ing, namely Gertrude Moore, di¬ 
rector of Moorecroft Camp on Van¬ 
couver Island. 

"Dinty”, as she was affectionately 
known to campers and counsellors 
alike, was born and educated in 
Toronto, a graduate of the Margaret 
Eaton School of Physical Education. 
She will be remembered as a water¬ 
front director at Glen Bernard 
Camp, as Director of Physical Ed¬ 
ucation at the Vancouver YWCA, 
and as Director of Women's Phys¬ 
ical Education at the University of 
British Columbia. 

Gertrude Moore opened her own 
camp for girls near Nanoose Bay in 
1934, the first private camp for 
girls in the West, and at her retire¬ 
ment sold the seventy-five acre site 
to the United Church of Canada. 
Today the church camp still oper¬ 
ates under the same name, "Moore¬ 
croft''. 

"Dinty" was the founder of the 
B.C. Camping Association in 1939, 
its first president, and at the time of 
her death she was Honorary Presi¬ 
dent. During the ten years in which 
she held executive office, many ad¬ 
vances were made in camping in 
British Columbia. The most impor¬ 
tant of these was the drawing up 
of standards for camping in that 
province in co-operation with the 
provincial government. Later this 
research and study was used as a 
basis for Government licensing of 
summer camps in B.C. 

Toronto camping people were 
privileged to meet with her when 
she visited Toronto a number of 
years ago. Her enthusiasm for 
camping and outdoor education 
overflowed, though she was then on 
the verge of retirement. She con¬ 
tributed many articles to Canadian 
Camping and after retirement in¬ 
spired the camping movement to go 
forward in her dream of providing 
a camping experience for every 
child, eventually including a camp¬ 
ing programme in the curriculum 
of the public schools in future. 

She will long be remembered 
with deep affection for the inspira¬ 
tion and encouragement she passed 
on to those in her charge, and for 
the enthusiasm she gave to the ad¬ 
vancement of good camping in the 
province of British Columbia. 

by Eanswythe Flynn
